detailedAnswer: API evolution is a compatibility contract, not just a code change: adding a method to an interface breaks existing implementors, changing a return type or generic signature breaks callers, and renaming a public type breaks everyone, so stable APIs evolve by addition and deprecation, not by modification. A plugin or extension architecture should therefore depend on narrow, versioned interfaces, use composition over inheritance so hosts are not coupled to plugin internals, and isolate plugins with their own classloaders when versions of a shared library must coexist. Reflection and serialization bypass normal access rules and type checks, so they belong at system boundaries with explicit schemas and validation, not scattered through business logic. When a breaking change is unavoidable, ship it behind a new major version with a migration guide, dual support during transition, and telemetry showing the old API is actually unused before removal.
followUps: Why does adding a method to an interface break implementors?
When is a classloader boundary worth its complexity?
question: How do you design a public Java API and plugin system that can evolve without breaking its consumers?
shortAnswer: Evolve by addition and deprecation, depend on narrow versioned interfaces, isolate plugins by classloader when needed, and remove old APIs only after telemetry proves they are unused.
tips: Frame compatibility as a contract, not a preference.
Name the interface-addition breakage — it is the classic trap.
title: API evolution and plugin design

detailedAnswer: At moderate scale the right collection is usually obvious, but at large scale the choice is driven by access pattern, memory overhead, and allocation behaviour, not by asymptotic complexity alone. An ArrayList of boxed objects costs far more memory and GC pressure than a primitive array or a specialized collection, a HashMap with a poor hash function degrades under adversarial keys, and a concurrent structure with high contention can be slower than a sharded or thread-local design. For ordered data, a balanced tree gives logarithmic ordered operations that a hash map cannot, and for streaming aggregation, a purpose-built accumulator avoids building intermediate collections entirely. The senior answer quantifies: estimate element count, per-element overhead, read-to-write ratio, and contention, then measure with a realistic workload, because a choice that is correct at ten thousand elements can be wrong at ten million.
followUps: When does a HashMap lose to a tree or a sorted array?
How do boxed primitives change the memory math?
question: How does collection choice change when a data structure must hold tens of millions of entries?
shortAnswer: Beyond asymptotic complexity, decide on memory overhead, allocation and GC pressure, hash quality, ordering needs, and contention, and measure at realistic scale.
tips: Quantify: element count, overhead, read-write ratio, contention.
Name boxing overhead as the hidden cost most candidates miss.
title: Collections at scale

detailedAnswer: Streams excel at declarative, in-memory transformation of finite data, but they are a poor fit for infinite or backpressured sources, for operations that need early exit with complex state, and for pipelines where checked exceptions or resource cleanup must be precise. A reactive stream, by contrast, models asynchronous data flow with demand signalling, so a slow consumer can slow the producer instead of being overwhelmed by an unbounded buffer. Mixing the two naively — collecting a reactive source into a list just to stream it, or blocking inside a reactive pipeline — loses the benefits of both. Choose plain streams for bounded in-memory work, reactive streams for asynchronous event flows with backpressure, and plain loops when the logic is stateful, exception-heavy, or performance-critical enough that stream overhead and boxing matter.
followUps: What does backpressure protect against that a plain stream cannot?
When is a plain loop better than a stream?
question: When should you not use Java Streams, and how does reactive streaming differ?
shortAnswer: Streams suit bounded in-memory transformation; reactive streams add demand signalling for async flows, and plain loops win for stateful, exception-heavy, or allocation-sensitive code.
tips: Define backpressure in one sentence before comparing.
Give a concrete anti-pattern: collecting a reactive source just to re-stream it.
title: Streams versus reactive streams

detailedAnswer: Lock-free algorithms use atomic compare-and-swap loops instead of locks, so a thread that fails a CAS retries rather than blocking, which avoids deadlock and keeps progress even when some threads stall, but retries under contention can burn CPU and the ABA problem can make a changed-then-restored value look unchanged. False sharing is the subtler trap: two threads updating different variables that share a cache line force the line to bounce between cores, so padding or grouping hot fields apart can yield large speedups in counters and queues. Distributed locking adds another layer: a lock held in Redis or a database must have a lease with expiry, a fencing token to reject stale holders after a pause, and a design that tolerates the lock holder dying, because a lock without expiry becomes a permanent outage. Prefer lock-free structures for single-JVM hot paths, and treat distributed locks as a coordination mechanism of last resort, with idempotent work underneath.
followUps: What is the ABA problem in a CAS loop?
Why does a distributed lock need a fencing token?
question: When do lock-free algorithms and distributed locks help, and what are their traps?
shortAnswer: Lock-free CAS avoids blocking but risks retry storms and ABA; false sharing punishes nearby hot fields; distributed locks need leases and fencing tokens and should sit above idempotent work.
tips: Pair each technique with its specific trap.
Mention fencing tokens — they separate experienced answers from textbook ones.
title: Lock-free and distributed locking

detailedAnswer: Low-latency collectors such as ZGC and Shenandoah keep pauses in the low milliseconds by doing most work concurrently with the application, at the cost of higher CPU overhead and throughput loss compared with G1 or Parallel. Tuning starts from a latency budget and a measurement: GC logs showing pause distribution, allocation rate, and heap occupancy, plus application latency percentiles, because average pause alone hides the tail that users feel. Escape analysis and JIT inlining reduce allocation in hot code, but they cannot rescue a design that allocates heavily per request, so the first optimization is usually fewer allocations, not more flags. For very large heaps or strict latency targets, evaluate the concurrent collector under production-like load and accept its CPU cost deliberately; for batch or throughput workloads, that trade is usually wrong.
followUps: Why is average GC pause a misleading metric?
When is a low-latency collector the wrong choice?
question: How do you choose and tune a garbage collector for a strict latency target?
shortAnswer: Start from a latency budget and percentile measurements; ZGC and Shenandoah buy millisecond pauses with CPU overhead, so use them for latency-sensitive services and reduce allocation before tuning flags.
tips: Insist on percentiles, not averages.
State the throughput cost explicitly — it is a trade, not a free win.
title: Low-latency GC tuning

detailedAnswer: Circular dependencies are usually a design smell: two beans needing each other at construction time means their responsibilities are tangled, and the honest fix is to extract the shared logic into a third bean or to invert the dependency. Spring can paper over some cycles with setter injection or proxies, but constructor injection rightly fails fast on a cycle, and suppressing that failure hides the design problem while making startup order fragile. Startup time in a large context comes from eager singleton creation, classpath scanning, and auto-configuration evaluation, so the remedies are lazy initialization for genuinely optional beans, narrower component scans, and fewer, more deliberate auto-configurations, measured with startup reports rather than guessed. For a modular monolith, enforce module boundaries with package rules and internal-only APIs, so the monolith stays decomposable instead of becoming a distributed monolith in disguise.
followUps: Why does constructor injection fail fast on a cycle while setter injection does not?
How do you keep a modular monolith decomposable?
question: How do you handle circular dependencies and slow startup in a large Spring application?
shortAnswer: Treat cycles as a design smell to refactor, not to suppress; constructor injection failing fast is a feature, and startup improves with lazy beans, narrow scans, and measured auto-configuration costs.
tips: Take a position: refactor the cycle, do not work around it.
Mention package-boundary rules for modular monoliths.
title: Circular dependencies and startup time

detailedAnswer: A custom starter should be a thin, opinionated packaging of auto-configuration, default properties, and dependencies, with every bean conditional so applications can override it, and with its own configuration properties namespace so settings do not collide. Multi-tenancy belongs in explicit layers: tenant resolution from a header or token, tenant-scoped data source routing or schema selection, and tenant context propagation through async boundaries, with tests that run the same scenario under two tenants. Observability is part of the starter contract: structured logs with correlation ids, metrics for the operations the starter performs, and health indicators that fail meaningfully rather than always reporting up. Graceful shutdown matters equally: stop accepting new work, drain in-flight requests within a timeout, and only then close resources, so rolling deploys do not drop requests.
followUps: How do you propagate tenant context across async boundaries?
What makes a health indicator meaningful rather than decorative?
question: How do you build a reusable Spring Boot starter for a multi-tenant platform?
shortAnswer: Keep starters thin and conditional with their own properties namespace, resolve tenant explicitly and propagate it through async work, and include observability and graceful shutdown as part of the contract.
tips: List the starter contract: conditional beans, namespace, observability, shutdown.
Name tenant propagation across async boundaries as the hard part.
title: Custom starters and multi-tenancy

detailedAnswer: API versioning is a compatibility strategy, not a URL prefix: version in the URI for coarse, client-visible breaking changes, in headers or content negotiation when clients can handle it, and prefer backwards-compatible evolution — additive fields, optional parameters, and tolerant readers — so most changes need no version at all. Contract tests, where consumers publish the expectations they rely on, catch breaking changes before release far more reliably than manual coordination, and a deprecation policy with sunset headers and usage telemetry tells you when an old version can actually be retired. Rate limiting and request validation belong at the gateway or filter layer for coarse protection, with fine-grained business limits in the service layer where domain context lives. Never version by forking controller code without a shared core, or the versions will drift and a bug fix will land in one version only.
followUps: When can you avoid versioning entirely?
How do you know when an old API version is safe to retire?
question: How do you version a public API and retire old versions without breaking clients?
shortAnswer: Prefer backwards-compatible evolution, version coarsely when breaking, enforce compatibility with consumer contract tests, and retire versions only on telemetry plus a published sunset policy.
tips: Lead with backwards-compatible evolution, not versioning schemes.
Name consumer contract tests as the enforcement mechanism.
title: API versioning and contract tests

detailedAnswer: JPA excels at single-database domain modelling, but it strains at scale in three places: a single write database becomes a bottleneck, a shared entity graph couples read and write shapes, and lazy loading plus the persistence context add overhead to bulk work. The standard responses are read replicas for read-heavy workloads with explicit tolerance for replication lag, CQRS read models that precompute the shapes queries actually need, and bulk operations through JDBC or batch statements that bypass the persistence context for imports and updates. Sharding is a last resort, not a first step, because it breaks joins, transactions, and reporting across shards and forces application-level routing and rebalancing. The senior judgement is knowing which scale problem you actually have — read volume, write volume, or data volume — because each has a different remedy.
followUps: When does a read replica hurt rather than help?
Why is sharding a last resort?
question: Where does JPA break down at scale, and what replaces each piece?
shortAnswer: Use read replicas for read volume, CQRS read models for mismatched read shapes, and JDBC batching for bulk work; reserve sharding for data volume it alone can solve, since it breaks joins and transactions.
tips: Diagnose the scale problem first: reads, writes, or data volume.
Warn that replication lag makes replicas unsuitable for read-after-write flows.
title: JPA at scale: replicas, CQRS, sharding

detailedAnswer: Event-driven architecture decouples producers from consumers in time and in topology, but it trades immediate consistency for eventual consistency, and that trade must be visible in the product: user interfaces need pending states, and business processes need compensations for late or failed events. Schema evolution is the long-term cost, so events should be versioned, backwards-compatible, and self-describing, with consumers tolerating unknown fields and producers never reusing a field name for a new meaning. Every consumer must be idempotent with a stored record of processed event ids, because at-least-once delivery guarantees duplicates, and every event flow needs dead-letter handling, replay capability, and distributed tracing across producer and consumer. If a workflow needs an immediate, synchronous answer, an event is the wrong tool — use a request-response call and reserve events for facts other services react to.
followUps: How do you make an event consumer safe to replay?
When is an event the wrong choice versus a synchronous call?
question: How do you design an event-driven system that survives duplicates, schema changes, and failures?
shortAnswer: Design for eventual consistency with pending states and compensations, version events compatibly, make consumers idempotent, and provide dead-letter handling, replay, and end-to-end tracing.
tips: Name the product consequence of eventual consistency, not just the pattern.
Insist on stored processed-event ids for idempotency.
title: Event-driven architecture at scale

detailedAnswer: At very large tables, query design is index design: range queries need the range column last in a composite index after equality columns, selective filters beat broad ones, and sorting without an index forces a costly sort of the full result. Partitioning by a natural key such as time lets old partitions be archived or dropped cheaply and keeps working sets small, but queries that do not filter on the partition key must scan every partition. Locking behaviour matters as much as speed: long transactions hold locks and block writers, gap locks under repeatable read can deadlock concurrent inserts, and the remedy is usually shorter transactions, consistent lock ordering, and retrying deadlocked transactions rather than raising timeouts. Always verify with the execution plan on production-sized data, because a plan that is fine at a million rows can be catastrophic at a hundred million.
followUps: Why should the range column come last in a composite index?
How do you reduce deadlocks without raising timeouts?
question: How do you design indexes, partitioning, and transactions for tables with hundreds of millions of rows?
shortAnswer: Order composite indexes equality-first and range-last, partition on the key queries actually filter by, keep transactions short with consistent lock ordering, and verify plans at production scale.
tips: Give the composite-index ordering rule concretely.
Name gap locks as the deadlock mechanism, not just deadlocks in general.
title: SQL at very large scale

detailedAnswer: The task is to design a rate limiter that works across multiple service instances. The idiomatic approach is a token-bucket or fixed-window counter per key, stored in a shared store with an atomic increment and expiry, so every instance observes the same count. A single-instance in-memory limiter is correct only until the second instance deploys, at which point each instance enforces its own limit and the effective limit multiplies. For strict fairness, use a shared atomic counter with a window, accept the small race window of fixed windows or the complexity of a sliding-window log, and return a standard too-many-requests response with a retry-after hint. Edge cases to name are clock skew between instances, hot keys that concentrate on one store shard, and the failure mode when the store itself is unavailable — fail open for non-critical endpoints, fail closed for abuse-sensitive ones.
followUps: Why does a per-instance limiter break when you scale out?
Should the limiter fail open or fail closed when its store is down?
question: Coding task: design a rate limiter that stays correct when the service scales to many instances. What is your approach?
shortAnswer: Use a shared atomic counter per key with a window in a central store, such as a token bucket, so all instances share one limit; per-instance counters multiply the limit on scale-out.
tips: Start from the scale-out failure of in-memory limiters.
Name the fail-open versus fail-closed decision for store outages.
title: Coding: distributed rate limiter

detailedAnswer: Apply the strangler pattern: put the new service behind the existing monolith's interface, route a slice of traffic or a single capability to it, and expand slice by slice, so every step is reversible and the old system remains the fallback. Data is the hard part: keep a single source of truth during transition, synchronize with change-data-capture or dual writes guarded by reconciliation jobs, and migrate data in small, verifiable batches with checksums rather than one big cutover. Rollback means routing traffic back and reconciling any writes the new service made, which only works if writes are idempotent and the old system can still accept them, so design the new service's writes with that constraint from day one. Success criteria are not the migration itself but the metrics that prove it: error rates, latency, and data-consistency checks at each slice, with a named owner and a decision point for each expansion.
followUps: Why is a big-bang cutover riskier than strangler migration?
How do you reconcile data written by the new service during rollback?
question: Scenario: you must extract a payment capability from a monolith into a service without downtime. How do you plan it?
shortAnswer: Strangle it slice by slice behind the old interface, keep one source of truth with reconciled synchronization, migrate data in verifiable batches, and make rollback possible via idempotent writes.
tips: Lead with the strangler pattern and reversibility.
Name data reconciliation, not just traffic routing, as the hard part.
title: Scenario: strangler migration

detailedAnswer: First, establish scope and reversibility: confirm the regression with a controlled comparison, such as canary traffic on the old and new versions under the same load, and check whether the change is the JDK, a library upgrade shipped with it, or a configuration change that rode along. Then narrow with evidence in order: GC logs and pause percentiles, JIT compilation and deoptimization logs, thread and CPU profiles, and dependency changelogs, looking for a behaviour change in a collector, a hashing order, or a default that the application silently depended on. As a staff-level decision, you would halt the rollout at the canary stage, keep the old version deployable, and choose between pinning the old version, tuning the new one, or fixing the application assumption, based on which evidence you have and how long each path takes. The post-incident action is a regression gate: a performance benchmark and a canary comparison in the upgrade pipeline, so the next JDK upgrade cannot regress silently.
followUps: How do you separate a JDK regression from a library or config change shipped with it?
When do you roll back versus tune forward?
question: Scenario: after a JDK upgrade, latency percentiles regress in production. As the technical lead, how do you investigate and decide?
shortAnswer: Compare canary versions under identical load, narrow with GC, JIT, and profile evidence, halt the rollout, and decide between rollback, tuning, or fixing the app assumption based on evidence and time to fix.
tips: Lead with the canary comparison, not with a guess about the collector.
Frame the decision explicitly: rollback, tune, or fix — with criteria.
title: Scenario: JDK upgrade regression
Coding: duplicate elements and their counts with streams
question: Coding task: given a list of integers, find the elements that appear more than once, together with how many times each appears, using the Stream API.
shortAnswer: Group the list by element with a count, then keep only the entries whose count is greater than one.
followUps: What is the time and memory cost of this approach?
How would you return the duplicates sorted by how often they appear?
tips: Name the two-step shape: group and count, then filter.
Walk through a small example so the interviewer sees the map taking shape.
commonMistakes: Sorting the list first and comparing neighbours, which is slower and more code.
Using a Set to detect duplicates but losing the counts the question asked for.

title: Coding: highest-paid employee per department with streams
question: Coding task: given a list of employees with a name, a department, and a salary, find the highest-paid employee in each department using the Stream API.
shortAnswer: Group by department, and inside each group reduce with maxBy on salary.
followUps: How would you unwrap the Optional in the result, and when is that safe?
What happens if two employees in one department share the top salary?
tips: Say the pattern name: a downstream collector inside groupingBy.
Name the tie behaviour before the interviewer asks.
commonMistakes: Sorting the whole list and taking the first per department, which is wasteful and fiddly.
Forgetting that maxBy returns an Optional and trying to use the result as a plain employee.

title: CountDownLatch versus CyclicBarrier
question: What is the difference between CountDownLatch and CyclicBarrier, and when would you pick each one?
shortAnswer: A latch is a one-shot gate that waits for a set of events; a barrier is a reusable meeting point where a set of threads wait for each other.
detailedAnswer:
A CountDownLatch is created with a count, other threads call countDown() as work finishes, and one or more waiting threads are released when the count reaches zero. It cannot be reset, so it fits one-off waits: a main thread waiting for several workers to finish initialising, or a test waiting for asynchronous callbacks. The waiting thread does not have to be one of the counting threads.

A CyclicBarrier is created with a number of parties, and every party must call await() before any of them is released, so the threads wait for each other rather than for outside events. It resets itself after each trip, so it fits repeated rounds of work, such as parallel computation that synchronises at the end of each step, and it can run a barrier action once per round when all parties arrive. A broken barrier, for example when a thread times out or is interrupted while waiting, trips the barrier for everyone, which is a failure mode a latch does not have.

The interview-ready rule: use a latch when one thread waits for many events to happen, and a barrier when many threads must arrive together before any of them continues.
followUps: What happens to a CyclicBarrier if one waiting thread is interrupted?
How would you wait for several services to finish starting up before taking traffic?
tips: Lead with the one-line contrast: one-shot gate versus reusable meeting point.
Give one concrete use for each instead of only describing the API.
commonMistakes: Saying the two are interchangeable because both make threads wait.
Forgetting that a latch cannot be reused and a barrier releases only when every party arrives.

title: ThreadPoolExecutor internals: sizing, queues, and rejection
question: Explain how ThreadPoolExecutor actually works inside: core threads, maximum threads, the work queue, and what happens when the pool is saturated.
shortAnswer: New tasks go to a core thread first, then to the queue, then to extra threads up to the maximum, and finally to the rejection policy; the queue type decides most of the behaviour.
detailedAnswer:
The order of decisions is the part most candidates get wrong. When a task arrives, the pool starts a new core thread if fewer than corePoolSize threads are running. Otherwise the task goes onto the work queue. Only when the queue is full does the pool grow beyond the core size, up to maximumPoolSize. If the pool is at its maximum and the queue is full, the rejection policy runs.

That makes the queue the most important sizing choice. An unbounded queue, which is what the Executors.newFixedThreadPool shortcut uses, means the pool never grows past its core size and can instead grow memory without bound under load, which is how services run out of memory during a slow downstream outage. A bounded queue with a sensible limit plus a rejection policy such as CallerRunsPolicy, which pushes back on the caller, or AbortPolicy with a clear error, gives you a visible, controllable failure instead.

Also name the supporting details: keep-alive time applies to threads above the core size, worker threads pull tasks from the queue in a loop, and a rejected task after shutdown is a separate case from a saturated pool. The senior answer ends with a rule of thumb: size core threads to the work, CPU-bound near the core count and I/O-bound higher, bound the queue, and choose the rejection policy deliberately.
followUps: Why can an unbounded queue make a fixed thread pool run out of memory?
When would you pick CallerRunsPolicy over AbortPolicy?
tips: State the order: core thread, then queue, then extra threads, then rejection.
Name the unbounded-queue trap in the Executors factory shortcuts.
commonMistakes: Saying the pool grows to its maximum before using the queue.
Treating the queue size as unimportant when it actually controls saturation behaviour.

title: Strong, soft, weak, and phantom references, and cache memory leaks
question: What are the four reference types in Java, and how do they explain the classic memory leak where a cache keeps growing forever?
shortAnswer: Strong references pin objects in memory; soft references are cleared under memory pressure, weak ones at the next collection, and phantom ones only signal cleanup. A cache of strong references is a leak by design.
detailedAnswer:
A strong reference is an ordinary reference: as long as it is reachable, the garbage collector will not reclaim the object. A soft reference is cleared when the JVM is short of memory, which makes it the right tool for a memory-sensitive cache. A weak reference is cleared at the next collection once no strong reference remains, which is how WeakHashMap lets entries disappear when their keys are no longer used elsewhere. A phantom reference cannot even be used to reach the object; it exists so cleanup code can be notified through a ReferenceQueue after the object is collected, and it is the mechanism behind the cleaner API that replaced finalizers.

The classic cache leak is a static map, or a long-lived collection, holding strong references to objects that are never removed: entries accumulate, the heap grows, and eventually the application fails with an OutOfMemoryError even though nothing is logically still needed. Other versions of the same leak are listeners that are never unregistered, ThreadLocal values left behind on pooled threads, and classloaders pinned by a single stray reference after a redeploy.

The fix depends on the intent: bound the cache with a size or time limit and an eviction policy, use soft or weak references where the cache is genuinely allowed to lose entries, and always remove what you registered. When diagnosing, look at what dominates the heap in a heap dump and follow the reference chain back to the GC root that keeps it alive.
followUps: When would you choose a soft reference over a weak reference for a cache?
How does a ThreadLocal leak happen on a pooled thread?
tips: Order the four types by how eagerly the collector clears them.
Trace the leak to a GC root in the heap dump, not just to the growing collection.
commonMistakes: Saying weak references are cleared only under memory pressure; that is soft references.
Treating a cache as harmless because it is only a map, while it holds strong references forever.

title: Dynamic proxies in Java and how Spring uses them
question: What are dynamic proxies in Java, how do you create one, and where does Spring rely on them?
shortAnswer: A dynamic proxy is a runtime-generated object that implements an interface and forwards every call to an InvocationHandler, which is how Spring adds behaviour such as transactions around a bean.
detailedAnswer:
A JDK dynamic proxy is created at runtime with Proxy.newProxyInstance, given a classloader, the interfaces to implement, and an InvocationHandler whose invoke method receives every method call. The handler can run code before and after the call, decide whether to call the real object at all, change arguments or results, and wrap exceptions. Because the proxy is built from interfaces, it can only stand in for an interface type, never for a concrete class.

Spring uses this mechanism in several places. Transactional methods, security checks, and asynchronous execution are applied by wrapping a bean in a proxy that adds the extra behaviour around the real method. When a bean implements an interface, Spring's default is a JDK dynamic proxy; when it does not, Spring falls back to a subclass-based proxy, historically CGLIB. That split explains two famous gotchas: a call from one method of a bean to another method of the same bean bypasses the proxy entirely, so a transactional annotation on the inner method is silently ignored, and final methods cannot be intercepted by a subclass proxy.

Good interview answers name a legitimate use of proxies beyond Spring: a logging or metrics wrapper, a lazy-loading stand-in, or a remote stub. They also name the cost: an extra indirection per call, stack traces that are harder to read, and behaviour that is invisible in the source code of the class itself.
followUps: Why does a self-call inside a bean skip transaction handling?
When does Spring switch from a JDK proxy to a subclass proxy?
tips: Start from the three inputs to newProxyInstance: classloader, interfaces, handler.
Connect the interface-only limit directly to the Spring self-invocation trap.
commonMistakes: Saying a dynamic proxy can wrap any class; it can only implement interfaces.
Forgetting that behaviour added by a proxy is invisible when reading the target class.

title: The Java module system (JPMS) for a modular monolith
question: How would you use the Java 9 module system to turn a monolith into a genuinely modular application, and what are the practical costs?
shortAnswer: Give each part a module-info file that declares what it needs and what it exports, so package boundaries become compiler-enforced instead of conventions.
detailedAnswer:
A module is a named group of packages with a module-info.java file. It declares requires for the modules it depends on and exports only the packages other modules may use; everything else is encapsulated, even public classes in non-exported packages. The opens directive exists for the frameworks that need deep reflection, such as serialization libraries and dependency injection containers, which is a deliberate hole you should keep as narrow as possible.

For a monolith, the practical path is to draw the boundaries first, usually one module per bounded context or layer, and then migrate bottom-up, starting with the libraries with the fewest dependencies, or top-down, starting with the application modules. Old jars without a module descriptor land on the classpath as the unnamed module or on the module path as automatic modules, which lets migration happen in stages, but split packages, where the same package exists in two jars, and reflective access from old frameworks are the two problems that actually block teams.

Be honest about the payoff at senior level: JPMS gives you strong encapsulation, a smaller runtime image with jlink, and reliable configuration that fails fast on a missing module, but it does not by itself give you a microservices architecture, and many teams decide the build and reflection friction is not worth it for an application that already enforces boundaries with build modules and package rules.
followUps: What is a split package, and why does JPMS refuse it?
When would you choose build modules over JPMS modules?
tips: Frame modules as compiler-enforced boundaries, not just packaging.
Name automatic modules as the realistic migration bridge.
commonMistakes: Claiming JPMS alone makes a system a microservices architecture.
Opening every package to reflection and defeating the encapsulation JPMS was added for.

title: Metaspace, PermGen, and diagnosing OutOfMemoryError
question: What is Metaspace, how does it differ from PermGen, and how would you investigate an OutOfMemoryError in production?
shortAnswer: Metaspace replaced PermGen in Java 8 and holds class metadata in native memory with no fixed default limit; an OutOfMemoryError there usually means classes or classloaders are leaking.
detailedAnswer:
Before Java 8, class metadata lived in PermGen, a fixed-size area inside the Java heap that filled up with too many classes and had to be tuned with PermSize and MaxPermSize. Since Java 8, the same metadata lives in Metaspace, which is allocated from native memory and by default grows until the operating system runs out of memory, with MaxMetaspaceSize as an optional cap. That removes the old tuning chore but changes the failure: Metaspace growth no longer throws a heap error, it consumes native memory, and the usual cause is a classloader leak, where a classloader and all its classes are pinned by a stray reference after a redeploy, or an application that generates classes without bound, such as dynamic proxies or runtime bytecode.

Investigating an OutOfMemoryError starts with which error it is, because the fix is different each time: Java heap space means live objects or a leak in the heap, GC overhead limit exceeded means the collector is spending nearly all its time collecting almost nothing, and Metaspace means classes or classloaders. Enable heap dumps on OutOfMemoryError so the evidence survives the crash, look at what dominates the heap or Metaspace in the dump, and check GC logs for the allocation and pause trend before the failure. A classloader leak shows up as many duplicate classloaders holding the same classes, and the fix is to find and break the reference that pins the old loader, not to raise a limit.
followUps: Why can raising MaxMetaspaceSize make a classloader leak worse instead of fixing it?
How do you tell a genuine heap shortage apart from a leak?
tips: Start by naming which OutOfMemoryError it is; the fixes are different.
Name the classloader leak as the classic Metaspace cause after redeploys.
commonMistakes: Raising the heap or Metaspace limit without finding what is growing.
Treating every OutOfMemoryError as a heap problem.

title: Spring AOP: join points, pointcuts, and where it breaks down
question: Explain Spring AOP in plain terms: join points, pointcuts, and advice, and when is AOP the wrong tool?
shortAnswer: AOP adds behaviour around method executions matched by a pointcut; it is proxy-based, so it only sees calls that pass through a Spring bean proxy.
detailedAnswer:
A join point is a point in the program where extra behaviour can be attached; in Spring AOP that is always a method execution. A pointcut is the expression that selects which methods match, for example all public methods in a service package. Advice is the extra behaviour itself, run before, after, or around the matched method, and an aspect is the class that bundles pointcuts and advice together.

Spring AOP works through proxies, which sets its limits. It can only intercept method calls on Spring beans that go through the proxy, so a call from one method to another method of the same bean bypasses the advice entirely, and it cannot intercept field access, constructors, or calls on objects Spring does not manage. Full AspectJ with compile-time or load-time weaving removes those limits but adds build complexity.

AOP earns its place for cross-cutting concerns that would otherwise be pasted into every method: logging, metrics, security checks, and transactions. It is the wrong tool when the behaviour is core business logic that belongs in the method itself, when the flow becomes hard to follow because behaviour is invisible at the call site, or when a simple decorator or an explicit call would say the same thing more clearly. The senior answer names the debugging cost directly: with AOP, reading a method no longer tells you everything that happens when it runs.
followUps: Why does a self-call inside a bean skip an aspect?
When would you reach for full AspectJ instead of Spring AOP?
tips: Define the three terms in one sentence each, then move to the limits.
Name the invisible-behaviour cost; it is the senior judgement.
commonMistakes: Saying AOP can intercept any code, including field access and constructors, in Spring.
Putting business logic in an aspect where nobody will look for it.

title: Caching done right: stale data, eviction, and stampedes
question: How do you use caching in a Spring Boot application without serving stale data or collapsing under a cache stampede?
shortAnswer: Cache with a short TTL and explicit eviction on writes, and make sure a cache miss is cheap or single-flighted so a cold cache cannot hammer the database.
detailedAnswer:
Spring's cache abstraction, @Cacheable to fill, @CacheEvict to clear, and @CachePut to refresh, is only the entry point; the real design is about invalidation. Every write path that changes the underlying data must evict or update the affected entries, or the cache will serve stale data until the time-to-live expires. A short TTL bounds how wrong the data can be, and versioning the cache key or the payload lets clients detect a stale read. Choosing a cache-aside pattern, where the application reads through the cache and fills it on a miss, keeps the database as the source of truth.

The second failure is the stampede: when a popular entry expires, many concurrent requests all miss at once and hit the database together. Mitigations are to refresh entries before they expire, to let one request refill while others wait briefly, or to stagger expiry times so entries do not all expire together. A local cache such as Caffeine is fast but is per-instance, so an eviction on one instance does not clear the others; a shared cache such as Redis is consistent across instances but adds a network hop and a new failure mode. The senior answer always names what happens when the cache is down: the application must fall back to the database, slowly, rather than failing every request.
followUps: Why is a local cache dangerous for eviction in a multi-instance service?
What should the application do when the cache itself is unavailable?
tips: Talk about invalidation before you talk about filling the cache.
Name the stampede as the failure that only appears at real traffic.
commonMistakes: Caching without an eviction path on writes and relying on TTL alone.
Treating a cache miss storm as a database problem instead of a caching design problem.

title: Zero-downtime deployment and safe rollback for Spring Boot
question: How do you deploy a new version of a Spring Boot service with zero downtime, and how do you roll back safely when the new version is bad?
shortAnswer: Roll out instance by instance behind readiness checks with graceful shutdown, keep database changes backwards compatible, and make rollback a redeploy of the known-good version.
detailedAnswer:
Zero downtime is a sequence, not a single feature. The new version starts, waits until it is genuinely ready, and only then receives traffic, which is what the readiness probe is for; a service that reports ready before its connections and caches are warm will fail its first real requests. The old instance stops accepting new work, finishes the requests it already has within a timeout, and only then shuts down, which is graceful shutdown, enabled with server.shutdown=graceful in Spring Boot. A rolling deploy repeats this one instance at a time, while blue-green and canary deploys add the ability to shift a slice of traffic and watch it before committing.

The part teams most often get wrong is the database. A new version must work with the old schema and the old version must work with the new schema during the transition, which is the expand-and-contract pattern: add a column first, deploy code that writes both shapes, then remove the old shape in a later release. A migration that renames or drops a column in the same deploy as the code that needs it is a guaranteed outage.

Rollback must be boring: redeploy the previous artifact, which only works if artifacts are versioned and the database change was backwards compatible. The decision to roll back should be made on metrics, error rate and latency at the canary stage, not on a feeling, and the runbook should say in advance who decides and how long the canary runs.
followUps: Why does a column rename break a rolling deploy?
What does the readiness probe check that the liveness probe does not?
tips: Walk the deploy as a sequence: ready, shift traffic, drain, stop.
Name expand-and-contract as the database rule.
commonMistakes: Reporting ready before the application can actually serve traffic.
Shipping a breaking database migration in the same release as the code that depends on it.

title: Distributed tracing: trace IDs, spans, and Micrometer Tracing
question: How does distributed tracing work in a Spring Boot microservice system, and what changed when Sleuth was replaced by Micrometer Tracing?
shortAnswer: Each request gets a trace ID shared by all services it touches, with a span per operation; Micrometer Tracing is the Boot 3 replacement for Sleuth that bridges to OpenTelemetry or Brave.
detailedAnswer:
A trace is the whole journey of one request across services, identified by a trace ID that is passed along in headers, and a span is one step in that journey, such as a controller call or a downstream request, identified by a span ID with a parent span ID linking it to the step that called it. With those three identifiers, logs and traces from many services can be joined into one timeline, which is what makes a slow request debuggable: you can see which service and which call actually consumed the time, instead of guessing from separate log files.

In Spring Boot 3, Sleuth was replaced by Micrometer Tracing. The concepts are the same, but the setup is different: you add Micrometer Tracing with a bridge to your tracing backend, OpenTelemetry or Brave, and a span exporter or collector such as Zipkin or an OpenTelemetry collector, and the trace and span IDs are put into the logging context automatically so every log line carries them. Sampling decides how many traces are recorded; keeping every trace is too expensive at scale, so production systems usually sample a fraction of normal traces and keep all error traces.

The practical pitfalls are propagation and context loss: the trace ID must travel across every hop, including message queues and asynchronous work, or the trace breaks into pieces, and a thread pool that does not copy the context will log work under the wrong trace. The senior answer names both and says how to check: follow one request end to end in the trace view and confirm no hop is missing.
followUps: Why do logs need the trace ID in them, not just the tracing UI?
What breaks tracing when work moves to another thread or a queue?
tips: Define trace, span, and the three IDs before describing any library.
Name sampling as the cost control, not an afterthought.
commonMistakes: Assuming tracing works automatically across async boundaries and message queues.
Keeping every trace in production and paying for it in storage and overhead.

title: WebFlux versus Spring MVC: when reactive is worth it
question: When should you choose Spring WebFlux over Spring MVC, and what is the mistake that ruins most first WebFlux projects?
shortAnswer: Choose WebFlux when many concurrent, mostly idle connections must share few threads; the classic mistake is blocking inside a reactive pipeline.
detailedAnswer:
Spring MVC gives each request a thread from a pool and blocks it while waiting for a database or a downstream call, which is simple and works well until the thread pool itself becomes the bottleneck. WebFlux runs on a small number of event-loop threads and never blocks them: work is expressed as publishers, Mono for zero or one result and Flux for many, and a thread picks up the next piece of work while an earlier one waits for I/O. That pays off for workloads with very high concurrency and lots of waiting, such as gateways, proxies, and streaming endpoints, where thousands of connections are open but mostly idle.

The mistake that ruins first WebFlux projects is blocking inside the pipeline: calling a blocking database driver, doing a slow computation, or taking a lock on an event-loop thread stalls every request sharing that thread. Blocking work must move to a dedicated scheduler for blocking calls or be replaced with a non-blocking client, such as a reactive database driver. Other honest costs are a harder debugging experience, with stack traces that cross asynchronous boundaries, and a smaller ecosystem of blocking libraries that need wrapping.

The senior rule is to choose on the workload, not on fashion: a typical CRUD service backed by a blocking database gains nothing from WebFlux and pays for complexity it does not need, while a gateway or a fan-out service with long-lived connections is where reactive earns its keep.
followUps: What happens if you call a blocking JDBC query inside a WebFlux handler?
How does backpressure protect a fast producer from a slow consumer?
tips: Lead with the workload shape, not the framework names.
Name the blocking-call mistake explicitly; interviewers wait for it.
commonMistakes: Adopting WebFlux for a standard CRUD service and gaining only complexity.
Blocking an event-loop thread and stalling unrelated requests.

title: Securing a REST API with JWT and OAuth2
question: How would you secure a REST API in Spring Boot end to end, using JWT and OAuth2, and what are the traps?
shortAnswer: Put TLS in front, authenticate with OAuth2 and short-lived signed JWTs, authorise by roles or scopes, and validate every token's signature, expiry, audience, and issuer.
detailedAnswer:
Start outside the code: the API is only reachable over TLS, tokens are never sent over plain HTTP, and the service sits behind rate limiting so a stolen token cannot be replayed at full speed. Authentication uses OAuth2: the client obtains a token from an authorization server, for example with the authorization code flow for users or the client credentials flow for services, and sends it as a bearer token. The resource server validates the token on every request: the signature against the authorization server's keys, the expiry, and the audience and issuer claims, so a token minted for another API or another environment is rejected.

A JWT is a signed container, not a vault: its header, payload, and signature are base64-encoded and readable by anyone, so it must never carry secrets or personal data, and its claims should be the minimum the API needs, such as the user id, roles, and scopes. Tokens are short-lived, with refresh tokens used to get new ones, and logout means the token simply expires, unless you keep a denylist, which is a trade-off most stateless designs accept. In Spring Boot this is configured as a resource server with a JWT decoder and method or URL rules that map scopes and roles to endpoints.

The traps to name: trusting a token without validating its signature, accepting tokens with no expiry, putting sensitive data in claims, and storing tokens in a place JavaScript can read when a cookie with the HttpOnly flag would have been safer.
followUps: How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?
Why must a JWT never contain secrets even though it is signed?
tips: Walk the request: TLS, token, validation, authorisation, in that order.
Say what a JWT is not: it is not encryption.
commonMistakes: Validating only that a token exists, not its signature, expiry, audience, and issuer.
Putting sensitive data into JWT claims because they look protected.

title: Service-to-service security in microservices
question: How do services authenticate and authorise each other in a microservices system, and why is a user token not enough?
shortAnswer: Give each service its own identity with short-lived credentials and mutual TLS, and check authorisation at every service, not just at the edge.
detailedAnswer:
A user token proves who the user is, but it says nothing about which service is calling, and once it is inside the network it can be passed along by any service, including one that was compromised. Each service therefore needs its own identity: mutual TLS, where both sides present certificates and verify each other, is the strongest common answer, and short-lived service tokens from the client credentials flow are the lighter alternative. Secrets and certificates come from a vault or a certificate manager with rotation, never from a config file checked into source control.

Authorisation must also be checked at every service, not only at the gateway: a service that trusts any internal caller is one breach away from full access, so each service verifies the caller's identity and whether that identity may perform the operation. The user token still travels with the request for user-level authorisation, but it is validated again at each hop rather than trusted because it arrived on an internal network.

The honest trade-offs are operational: certificate rotation, clock skew between services, and debugging a request that fails authentication in the middle of a chain. The senior answer names a concrete check for the design: revoke one service's credentials and confirm that exactly that service loses access while everything else keeps working.
followUps: Why is trusting the internal network alone not a security model?
How would you test that revoking one service's credentials works?
tips: Separate the two identities: the user and the calling service.
Name the revocation test as proof the design works.
commonMistakes: Passing the user token along and treating any internal call as trusted.
Hard-coding service secrets in configuration files.

title: Database per service: the trade-offs and the consistency bill
question: Why does each microservice get its own database, and what do you lose when you can no longer join across services?
shortAnswer: A private database keeps services independently deployable and scalable, but cross-service joins and transactions become API calls, events, or sagas.
detailedAnswer:
A private database per service is what makes services genuinely independent: one team can change its schema, scale its storage, or even pick a different database technology without coordinating a shared schema change with every other team, and a failure or a heavy query in one service cannot lock tables that another service needs. A shared database quietly re-couples services that look independent on a diagram, because every schema change becomes a negotiation.

The bill arrives in three places. First, reading data that lives in two services can no longer be a join; it becomes an API call, a replicated read model, or a query service that joins data it has copied. Second, a write that spans services can no longer be one transaction; it becomes a saga with compensating actions or an outbox that publishes an event after the local commit. Third, reporting across services needs its own pipeline, because there is no single database to query.

The judgement call is to choose the mechanism per use case: synchronous API calls when the caller needs an immediate answer, events and replicated read models when eventual consistency is acceptable, and a saga when a multi-step write must be undone cleanly. The interview answer that stands out names the consistency the business actually needs before picking a mechanism, because most cross-service reads tolerate a short delay, and the ones that do not should be designed as a single service boundary instead.
followUps: When would you accept a shared database despite the coupling?
How do you build a report that needs data from five services?
tips: Start with the independence the pattern buys, then present the bill.
Pick the mechanism from the consistency the business needs.
commonMistakes: Reaching for a distributed transaction as the first answer to cross-service writes.
Joining across services by giving one service direct access to another's tables.

title: The API Gateway pattern: what it owns and what breaks it
question: What does an API Gateway do in a microservices architecture, and what goes wrong when it owns too much?
shortAnswer: The gateway is the single entry point that routes, authenticates, rate-limits, and aggregates; it breaks when business logic or service-specific rules creep into it.
detailedAnswer:
Clients talk to one stable address, and the gateway routes each request to the right service, terminates TLS, checks authentication, enforces rate limits, and adds cross-cutting behaviour such as request logging, correlation IDs, and response caching. It can also aggregate several downstream calls into one response for a client, which is the backend-for-frontend variant, where each client type gets a gateway tailored to its needs.

The gateway earns its place by removing duplicated plumbing from every service, but it has two failure modes. The first is availability: it is a single entry point, so it must itself be deployed redundantly and must fail gracefully, shedding load rather than taking the whole system down. The second is scope creep: when business logic, service-specific validation, or data transformation moves into the gateway, it becomes a distributed monolith that every team must change and that no team owns. Routing, security, and traffic policy belong in the gateway; domain rules belong in the services.

A good answer also names the alternative: direct client-to-service calls with service discovery, which removes the hop and the bottleneck but pushes routing, authentication, and versioning onto every client. The choice is a trade-off between a central choke point with consistent policy and a decentralised design with duplicated client logic.
followUps: When would you use a backend-for-frontend instead of one shared gateway?
How do you keep the gateway itself highly available?
tips: List what the gateway owns, then draw the line where its ownership stops.
Name the alternative so the trade-off is visible.
commonMistakes: Putting domain logic in the gateway until it becomes a monolith in disguise.
Treating the gateway as free and forgetting it adds latency and a failure point.

title: Scenario: rescuing a project that is slipping badly
question: Scenario: as the technical lead, you inherit a project that is weeks behind schedule with low morale and no clear picture of what is actually done. How do you recover it?
shortAnswer: First get a truthful picture of what is done and what is blocking, then cut scope with stakeholders, stabilise the plan in short cycles, and protect the team from further churn.
detailedAnswer:
The first move is diagnosis, not heroics: build an honest inventory of what is genuinely finished, what is half done, and what is blocked, by looking at the work itself rather than status reports, and talk to the team privately to learn what is actually slowing them down. A project that is behind usually has a small number of real blockers, such as an unclear requirement, a flaky dependency, or one overloaded person, hiding behind a long list of tasks.

The second move is to re-plan with stakeholders, not for them: present the real state, offer explicit trade-offs between scope, date, and quality, and agree a smaller, credible scope with a short, visible cadence, such as weekly demonstrable progress, so trust is rebuilt with evidence rather than promises. Cutting scope is a decision stakeholders must own; silently dropping quality is not a recovery plan.

The third move is to protect the team's ability to deliver: remove or sequence the blockers, limit work in progress so half-finished work stops multiplying, and stop adding new scope until the plan is stable. Morale recovers when people see progress and when overtime is not the plan. The answer that stands out names the trap explicitly: adding more people to a late project usually slows it further while they learn the codebase, so the recovery is about focus and unblocking, not headcount.
followUps: How do you tell stakeholders the date will slip without losing their trust?
What do you do if the main blocker is a person the project depends on?
tips: Lead with diagnosis from the work itself, not from status reports.
Make scope cuts an explicit stakeholder decision, not a silent quality cut.
commonMistakes: Adding people to a late project as the first response.
Promising a new date before finding out what is actually unfinished.

title: Scenario: handling scope creep and aligning tech with business goals
question: Scenario: stakeholders keep adding features mid-sprint while the deadline stays fixed. As a senior developer and tech lead, how do you handle it, and how do you keep technical work aligned with business goals?
shortAnswer: Make every addition an explicit trade-off: estimate its cost, show what it displaces, and let stakeholders choose, tying each item to the business outcome it serves.
detailedAnswer:
Scope creep is rarely malice; it is usually a request that sounds small and whose cost is invisible. The response is to make the cost visible: estimate the new work honestly, show what would have to be dropped or delayed to fit it in, and put the choice back to the stakeholders instead of absorbing it silently. A simple rule helps: new work enters through the same prioritisation as existing work, and nothing jumps the queue without displacing something.

Alignment with business goals works the same way, by translation. A technical item earns its place by the business outcome it serves: a refactoring that unblocks a revenue feature, a performance fix that reduces churn, or a reliability investment that protects a launch. When you present technical work in those terms, stakeholders can weigh it against features fairly, and you stop being the person who says no and become the person who shows the trade-off.

The practices that make this stick are a short written change note for any mid-sprint addition, a visible backlog ordered by value rather than by who shouted loudest, and a habit of revisiting the original goal when a request arrives, because a request that does not serve the goal is easy to defer once the goal is in the room.
followUps: What do you do when a stakeholder insists the addition is urgent and free?
How do you justify a refactoring to a non-technical stakeholder?
tips: Turn every addition into a visible trade-off instead of a yes or no.
Translate technical work into the business outcome it protects.
commonMistakes: Absorbing extra work silently and then missing the deadline.
Arguing technical merit instead of business value when asking for engineering time.

title: Scenario: mentoring juniors and explaining tech to non-technical stakeholders
question: Scenario: you are the senior on a team with junior developers, and you must also explain a risky technical decision to non-technical stakeholders. How do you handle both?
shortAnswer: Mentor through small, reviewed, real work with clear goals; explain technical decisions to stakeholders in terms of risk, cost, and options, not implementation details.
detailedAnswer:
Mentoring works through real work, not lectures. Give a junior a small, well-bounded task with a clear definition of done, review the work promptly with reasons rather than verdicts, and pair on the hard part so they see how a senior thinks through it, including the dead ends. Set a visible growth goal, such as owning a small feature end to end, and protect time for it instead of letting urgent work crowd it out every sprint. The signal that mentoring is working is independence: the junior starts asking better questions and needs fewer reviews for the same kind of task.

Explaining a risky decision to non-technical stakeholders uses the same discipline in reverse: start with the outcome and the risk, not the technology. Say what happens if you do it and if you do not, what it costs in time and money, and what the alternatives are, in plain language without jargon. A useful shape is options with trade-offs: the safe option, the fast option, and the recommended option, with the recommendation justified by the business risk it reduces. Invite questions rather than presenting a finished decision, because a stakeholder who understands the trade-off will defend it later.

Both jobs share one habit: check understanding instead of assuming it. Ask the junior to explain the design back to you, and ask stakeholders what worries them about the plan, because the worry they name is the one your explanation must answer.
followUps: How do you know when a junior is ready to own a feature alone?
What do you do when stakeholders reject your recommended option?
tips: Mentor with real tasks and prompt, reasoned reviews.
Present decisions as options with trade-offs, in business language.
commonMistakes: Mentoring only by reviewing finished code instead of pairing on the thinking.
Explaining the implementation instead of the risk, cost, and options.
